en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yu of Fanchang Chan Monastery in Fenning, Hongzhou.
By Xu Fu of Nanzhou.
Among those who today occupy monasteries as elders, gathering disciples and styling themselves as world-transcending patriarchs, there is no knowing how many there may be.
When people in their daily lives engage in discourses of exhortation and dialogue, their disciples invariably record them, calling these "Recorded Sayings" (yulu).
While the words of these recorded sayings fill the world, the Buddha-dharma becomes increasingly obscure. Is it not because an abundance of words leads one further away from the Way?
Is a painted cake not sufficient to satisfy hunger? Indeed, those who can speak eloquently are not necessarily those who truly embody the Way.
To know the depth or shallowness of one's realization, one must observe whether that person is virtuous or not.
In the past, the old master Fachang wore coarse clothing and ate simple food; he was as pure and refined as ice or jade. He used his hoe to provide for the traveling monks from all quarters.
Among scholars, none could match him in his diligent labors, yet they found his austere and simple life so bitter that they all fled from him in haste until the hall was empty.
When my late father was young, he was not yet known to the world; it was Master Shi alone who recognized his extraordinary talent.
As the local people came to respect Master Shi, it was from my late father’s time that the friendship between these two men began and grew into a profound bond. My late father’s...

His voice and countenance are now far removed. For thirty years, there has been no more of this elder’s refined spirit. When one longs for such a person yet cannot see them, how could his words be discarded?
Thus, they have been carved into woodblocks and circulated. Preface on the twenty-second day of the first month in the fourth year of Chongning.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yu of Fanchang Chan Monastery in Fenning, Hongzhou, compiled by his junior disciple Zongmi.
On the day the Master ascended the hall, after the proclamation of the sutra had concluded, he took his seat and held up the incense, saying: "This one portion of incense is offered for..."

For the present Emperor, the Son of Heaven, we pray for the prolongation of his sacred longevity. We humbly wish that the Dragon Chart may remain forever firm, the Phoenix Calendar ever renewed, the four seas eternally peaceful and clear, and the Wheel of Dharma constantly turning.
Again, holding up the incense, he said: "This single offering of incense is respectfully offered for the Chancellor, the Academician, and all the officials of the prefecture.
We pray that their mountain of longevity may grow ever more lofty and their ocean of merit ever more profound, so that they may forever serve as the sovereign’s pillars."

[The Master] raised his arm. He acted as a protector of the Zen school from outside its ranks. Again, he held up the incense and said: "This single portion of incense—the names of the Buddhas of the three periods are unknown to it;

the countenances of the patriarchs of successive generations are unrecognized by it. It does not come from the Dragon Palace or the Ocean Treasury, nor is it from the Tiger’s Den or the Demon’s Abode.
Is there anyone who knows its place of origin? I offer it in honor of Chan Master Xian of Beichan in Tanzhou."
Incense was burned in the incense burner. Whether they heard it or saw it, all attained the True Constant. Then, he adjusted his robes and sat down. The *vinaya-dhara* struck the gavel and said:
"O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). The Master said: "What excellent news! Is there anyone here who recognizes it?
If not, ask whatever doubts you have. A monk asked: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they emerge from the earth."
Jinlian asked, "When a monk appears in the world, what auspicious signs are there? The Master said, "Striking a golden bell atop Mount Sumeru.
Jinlian further asked, "In that case, today I have heard what I had not heard before. The Master said, "As for the matter of hearing, how is it?
Jinlian replied, "It is not only Avalokiteśvara; I too have realized it from within. The Master said, "To have eyes yet be like one blind is still somewhat tolerable."
[The Master] said, "To have ears and yet be like one deaf is enough to kill people with laughter.

The student asked, "If Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born, at this very moment, how can one discuss the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "It is all on the tip of Farchang’s staff.
The student asked, "Why do I, a student, not understand? The Master said, "The bright sun is in the sky; the blind man feels for the ground. The student asked, "..."
"If it is so, then the great assembly shall receive your grace. The Master said, "What principle have you seen? The monk replied, "I wish to speak, but words fail me;
let us deliberate well beneath the forest trees. The Master said, "You are a confused lot, monks as numerous as hemp and millet.
A monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he first delivered the five bhikṣus. When you, Master, appear in the world, whom do you deliver first?"
The Master said, "Following the mud to create a Buddha. The student asked, "I am currently lost on the path; why does the Master not grant me a skillful means?
The Master picked up his staff and asked, "Do you see it? The student replied, "I see it. The Master said, "Do not say there are no skillful means.
The student asked, "Is this not precisely where the Master benefits others? The Master set down the staff, and the monk prostrated.
[The monk] prostrated. The Master said, "Studying the Tang steps in Handan. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Patriarch’s intent coming from the West;
how is it with the matter of ascending the hall to expound the Dharma? The Master said, "Everyday tea and rice. The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then one exerts effort but gains no merit.
The Master said, "Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray it are many. The monk pressed further, "A single phrase, spiritual and resonant, transcends all."
[The Master] said, "This image stands far beyond the Three Vehicles and requires no cultivation.
The Master said, "For now, do not be so hasty. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Fachang? The Master said, "The earth is numinous; at every step there is the grass of the Snowy Mountains.

The monk followed up, "In that case, every person is a jewel of the Sangha, like a pearl from the blue sea. The Master said, "If everyone were like this monk, how much effort would be saved! The monk followed up, "Beyond this, is there still..."
[The monk] asked, "Is there anything? The Master said, "There is nothing even below. [The monk] further asked, "What kind of mental activity does the Master have?
The Master said, "A good heart does not receive a good reward. A monk asked, "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive."
The drum was beaten and [the master] ascended the hall. "What matter is to be addressed now?

The Master said, "First, I pray for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-year reign; second, I pray for the high ministers’ thousand-year prosperity. The questioner said, "That is still just the circulation of worldly truths.

As for the matter of the Zen school, how about that? The Master said, "His mouth is like a stone pillar base. The questioner said, "Why is it so? The Master said: *Note: The dialogue reflects the classic Chan style of direct, paradoxical response intended to test and provoke insight beyond conventional logic.*
"I dare not violate the strict command of the *ācārya*. The student asked, "Wherein lies your compassion? The Master said, "Have you not heard it said:

'Stop, stop! There is no need to speak'? The student asked, "Before the colors of dawn have even parted, all gaze upward; yet when day breaks, it is as usual. The Master said, "One reaps what one sows."
The Master then said: "Cease this questioning and discussion for a moment. Before any signs of good or ill fortune have appeared, there is already much complication.
Why go further with such free-flowing questions and answers? They only lead further astray and further away. Why is this? The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and transcends all names and forms.

Originally, there were no worlds and no sentient beings. Because of delusion, there is birth; because of birth, there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth. (Third)
The Buddhas of the world, upon reaching this point, have no leisure to gaze upward; the entire Great Canon of teachings cannot fully express its meaning.
For this reason, the Elder of Vaiśālī closed his mouth and remained speechless, while the Honored Hero of Magadha hung his tongue in awe of the wind.

Even if the Great Vehicle of the School were fully opened and the Patriarchal Command were being enacted—cutting off all conceptualization, transcending all realms of existence, attaining realization at the blow of the staff, or under a shout—[it would still not suffice].
To accept [this burden] and proclaim it within the Gate of the Way—such a person, when scrutinized, is much like one scratching an itch through a boot.
Do you not see that when the former Master [Baoshou] opened the hall, Sansheng pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou struck him immediately?
Sansheng’s way of acting for others did not merely blind this one monk; he blinded the entire city of Zhenzhou.
Baoshou then cast down his staff and returned to his quarters. O worthy ones, such was the single occasion of the ancients’ teaching.
In receiving beings and benefiting sentient life, there have thus been such extraordinary matters; for a thousand ages hence, these shall resound like jade and metal.
Thus, affairs do not follow a single direction, and principles emerge from many paths. It is just as Fa-chang today opens the hall for the sake of the nation.
How could there not be benefit? I venture to ask you all: regarding the many questions and answers just now, tell me, were they the same as those of Master Baoshou, or were they different?
If you say they were the same, then the golden sand has not yet been distinguished and the jade has not yet been separated; where, then, lies the eye of a student of the Way?
If you say they were different, the Ultimate Way is without difficulty—it only dislikes discrimination. How could there be [duality] in the Buddha-Dharma?
"Are there two? Is there anyone who can clarify this here? After a long silence, he said: "The moon in the empty realm over the azure pool for ten thousand ages;
only after repeatedly searching and grasping will you begin to know. (The words of thanks are not recorded.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before Śākyamuni had passed away and before Kāśyapa had heard [the teaching], those who entered the holy from the ordinary did so with no wasted effort.

The texts of the Great Canon are like gold and jade; yet when it came to the Golden-Colored Dhūta receiving the Dharma and transmitting the robe, they could find no place to emerge within the Dragon Palace or the oceanic treasuries.
But tell me, what excellence does the Patriarch possess? A single pill cures all ailments."
There are many false prescriptions for the Way.
He ascended the hall and said: "If you withdraw a thousand feet, I shall sprout right where you stand.
If you present yourself face-to-face, I shall hide my body and play with shadows. If you pick up pebbles from a spring pond, I shall scatter bright pearls. Directly...
It is such that water poured upon it does not stick, and the wind cannot penetrate it; it is like a solid iron hammer without a hole.
Tell me, does Fachang have any way to benefit others? When a sharp blade cuts the flesh, the wound may still heal; but when harsh words injure a person, the resentment never fades.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring mountains are green, the spring waters are azure. A single awakening after a spring nap in the realm of Nako is complete.

Grasping my staff, I stride forth through the pine gate; everywhere I pluck blossoms, their fragrance rich and pervasive. Reflecting thus, I think of the old Master Lingyun of old, who for thirty years could find no trace of it.
Now everyone vies to pluck the willow flowers; red fragrance fills the ground, yet no one sweeps it up.
Ascending the hall, he said: "No sun in spring, no rain in summer; the rice is not rice, and the millet is not millet.
In vain do you say that your grandsons understand plowing and weeding; yet without the timing of Heaven, one suffers in toil. Do not suffer! Look, look—soon there will be the autumn rains."

Fachang is no expert at interpreting celestial omens; yet, in the darkness, there are naturally dragon deities to protect him. He ascended the hall. The Master said, "Where is the mirror? The monk drew a circle. The Master then struck him, saying: "Even if you polish it for ten thousand years, It will never become bright. "This lacquer bucket—[he] does not even recognize the brick. The Master then said:
"The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing this matter, solely so that people of the time would know it exists. It is like the poor man’s jewel in his clothing;
it was not obtained from another. The Buddhas of the three periods are merely those who play with the jewel. As for the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages..."
"You are precisely those people who seek jewels at the bottom of the sea; you are but wandering beggars—people who carry treasures within their own countries yet remain lost.
To a man of keen intelligence, as soon as someone mentions it, he raises his eyebrows and immediately knows its whereabouts.
If you continue to step forward, it would be better to take up your staff and return to the mountains, letting out a long啸 (shout) as the mist deepens."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Where does a person who knows 'there is' ultimately go? The Master said, "Sweep the snow from your own door yourself;
do not concern yourself with the frost upon another's roof. The monk pressed further, "I want everyone to know this too. The Master said:
"There is no need to laboriously hang up the stone mirror; when dawn breaks, the rooster cries of itself. The monk said, "How can you, Master, meet me with such weapons?
The Master said, "When hungry, one encounters a king’s banquet but cannot eat it. The monk said, "Do not suppress the noble to become the base.
The Master said, "Tell me, where does a person who truly knows go? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Do not say 'suppressing the noble'."
[The student] was dejected. The Master then said: "There is no need for frantic seeking; recognize this as your livelihood. Gold does not trade with gold; water does not wash water.
The crooked does not hide the straight; the true does not mask the false. An elephant’s trunk and a pig’s head; fish gills and a bird’s beak. What more is there to ask? Return home."

While the assembly was dozing during the formal session, the Master ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season. Those who nest in trees know the wind;
those who dwell in burrows know the rain. Swallows depart and geese arrive; cold and heat alternate in turn. All people know this is so. But tell me, when the World-Honored One held up the flower—"
Kāśyapa smiled. "What season is this? Do you understand? Cold as ice, white as snow, here it forms a mound, its light brilliant and pure.
Vastly spreading, the fire of desire seeks to burn people; in deep regret and for no other reason, I speak for your sake."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today, the fifth day, I ascend the hall not to discuss the profound or expound the subtle. Space itself has its own dragons and spirits;
who asks whether the monks are many or few?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "I have heard that on Mount Fanchang, there are usually many fierce tigers. They devour dogs and sheep, leaving no foxes or hares behind;
they even injure travelers by day, numbering three, four, or five. Now that I have become a mountain dweller, I must act as the master of the mountain.
To the spirits of the monastery grounds and the gods of the five supernatural powers: from this day forward, you must patrol and protect this place; at dawn, drive them away."
He goes out toward another mountain, instructing him to eat both mud and earth. The incense, lamps, gruel, and rice have never been lacking; how could such things ever serve as a main road?
Yet he must take the road; I shall send you to the summit of the front mountain to ride upon the wind and rain.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single thread does not form a line; a solitary palm does not produce a sound. Why did Bodhidharma return to the West with only one shoe?
Even if you can utter a phrase that reveals your true self, I shall still ask you: what was the intention of the ancients? After a long silence, he said:
"Riding a donkey while wearing a straw hat; crossing water without wearing boots."
Ascending the hall on the first day of spring, he said: "The painted horns atop the lofty tower announce that spring has returned; The warm sun secretly blows, and the lotus faces open.
Among those with heads and horns dwelling in their hibernation caves, How many can remain indifferent as they await the wind and thunder?"
When Chan Master Huanglong Nan arrived, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is it like when two dragons struggle for the pearl?
The Master said, "Fachang makes a small exit and meets with a great encounter. The monk pressed further, "If suddenly the mountain torrents overflow and the peaks collapse, what then?
The Master struck him. The monk continued, "There is a question and there is an answer; why do you not distinguish between guest and host? The Master said, "Just now, one..."

[The Master] strikes with the staff. [The monk] asks, "Who is the guest? Who is the host? He steps forward and says, "This student shares it with the Master. The Master says, "This lacquer bucket is struck again!
He steps forward and says, "Were it not for the fisherman’s guidance, how could one see the surging waves? The Master says, "Do not be so dull-witted, Huanglong."
The monk prostrated. The Master said, "He was told to desist, yet he refused to desist. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials;
what is the 'house style' of Shao Shi like? The Master said, "Those within the dust do not recognize it; the traveler beyond the clouds knows it first.
The monk stepped forward and asked, "Is this the lid fitting the vessel within the heavens? Or is it following the waves and drifting with the currents? The Master said, "Strike as you please."
[The Master] hit a tile with a brick. The student asked, "Why does the Master hold fast to the boundaries?
The Master said, "Not knowing how to row the boat, you instead resent the winding of the stream. The student asked, "I do not know where Yunmen’s wooden horse neighs.
The Master said, "It is inside your nostrils. The student asked, "If it has nostrils, let that be; but if it has no nostrils, where would it be? The Master—
The Master said, "What a fine monk! He truly has no nostrils. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "In the furnace and forge, dull iron is most abundant.
The Master then continued, "Those who seize the clouds and grasp the waves are as numerous as hemp seeds; yet when their coppery eyes are struck, they go blind.
Apart from the head and horns of the Yellow Dragon, everything else is nothing but red-spotted snakes. This is a small monastery, Fa-chang; the road is long and the mountains [distant]."
Remote and secluded, its scenery is desolate and few travelers venture there. I dare say that the Venerable Master Huanglong has condescended to grace us with his presence;

not only do the springs and rocks thereby gain luster, but even the dragons and devas are filled with joy. Indeed, the movement of clouds and the falling of rain have been thus from ancient times until now.
Yet, alas, there are many pieces of dull iron within the furnace; at the gate of a skilled physician, the patients are most severe.
To cure an illness, one must seek the divine medicine; to melt away stubbornness, one must rely on the golden hammer. Here at Fachang, there are several masters whose roots have fallen away;
the sick are ill beyond the *gao* and *huang*, and the stubborn have become as hardened as the marrow of their bones. Were it not for the old fellow Huanglong arriving...
"Come! You have all lived in vain and died in vain. He then picked up his staff and said, "Do you understand? To make noodles, one must use the wheat from that very province;
to sing the song, one must be a man from the imperial capital."
Wearing a flowered kerchief upon his head, he left Shaoshi; carrying a straw hat in his hand, he departed Chang’an.
Once again we meet beneath Vulture Peak; our nostrils have always been exactly the same. (Huanglong)
A winter melon hangs from a gourd arbor; a shrimp is caught amidst waves of ripening wheat. Who is there at the painted tower where wine is sold?
Inviting one another to come drink Zhaozhou’s tea. (Fachang)
Pairs of iron oxen with golden horns; pairs of wooden horses with white jade hooves.
Out of love for the fine fragrant grasses of the Snow Mountains, they ride the moon at night across the stream before them. (Huanglong)
The Jade Unicorn, girded by the moon, leaves the Milky Way; the Golden Phoenix, clutching flowers, descends from the painted pavilion.
The rustic old man does not disdain the young lord’s intoxication; together they walk hand-in-hand through the Imperial Street. (Fachang)
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
The Master said: "Wait, wait! Fachang has a treasure: the seven perversions and eight inversions. Sometimes it becomes the mountain of ignorance;
sometimes it manifests as the physical marks and signs. It shines brilliantly everywhere, yet as soon as one moves, one enters the wild weeds—do not seek it out! It is a branch of coral."
On the first day of the month, the sun shone brightly. He ascended the hall and said:

"Night after night one embraces the Buddha while asleep; morning after morning one rises together with him. Rising and sitting, we always follow one another; speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together.
If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech. The ancient Buddhas bestowed their compassion; there was no lack of means.

Alas! Though it be a good cause, how can one help but encounter an evil result? Master Fu [Tao-shih] was like one who spread a vast net across the heavens to scoop up dragons and strike down phoenixes;
yet alas, all those with scales and shells, feathers and fur, were caught within its confines, with no way to escape their lives.
Only the auspicious birds and rare beasts would surely have found another realm of existence.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall and said: "When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, was born in Kapilavastu, nine dragons spat forth water and the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers.
Pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, he declared, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
This was much like being insolent and indifferent to others. But when the old fellow of Shaoyang came forward and struck him with a staff—"

Everyone everywhere thought that [the Dharma] would crumble like ice melting; little did they know that when Heaven intends for light, there must first be darkness, and when a person intends for prosperity, there must first be decline.
It is like a drum smeared with lethal poison: once struck, all goes awry.

This has caused the ancestral domain, for a thousand autumns, to see the raising of weapons in competition, becoming a subject of gossip on people's lips. Facha was undaunted even in the face of peril—what a fine "thump," yet it was far too late!
When he was born, before he had left Tuṣita Heaven, one ought to have struck him with a single blow beneath the heels; how could it have reached this day?
Even so, it is much like drawing a bow after a thief has already passed. Is there anyone who can utter a word here that turns the situation once, without harming the essential meaning of things?
This would not only vent the frustration of Gautama, but would also cut through the entanglements of all quarters. Is there such a person? Do not hesitate!
I find him strangely full of self-importance; his house has already trodden upon the highest pass. He ascended the hall and said:
"The three realms are but mind—here the four propositions cease. The myriad conditions are but consciousness—here the hundred negations are removed.
If there is even one dharma remaining, attachment cannot be avoided; when not even one dharma remains, that too is dispelled. When the ancients spoke thus, it was much like sending off [a guest].
A man has climbed a tree and removed the ladder; better that the good deed had not been done at all. Why?
The Buddha taught all dharmas to deliver all minds. Since I have no mind, what use are all dharmas?
Today, Fachang does not spare his own life for your sakes; I have set up the ladder. Those who can descend shall not be refused the four types of offerings, however laborious they may be.
"One who cannot grasp it below can even exhaust ten thousand taels of gold for it; let the man of clear eyes discern and take it. After a long silence, he said:
"Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The clouds have gathered in the vast fields; the moon is bright in the long sky. Woodcutters sing as they traverse the crags; fishermen chant by the reeds on the banks.
The myriad phenomena of the forest and the heavens intermingle their light like the celestial net of Indra. The four sages and six classes of beings are all reflected in the layered Sea-Seal.

The pavilions of Samantabhadra stretch across the ten directions. Yet, before the Peak of Shaoshi, they cannot even meet at a single point. Why is this? It is like the lute, the harp, and the *konghou*—though..."
There is a wondrous sound, yet without wondrous fingers, it can never be produced. Arriving at this point, I ask:
is there any monk who would blow a holeless flute or tune a stringless lute? Try, for the sake of Fachang, applying wondrous fingers to produce that wondrous sound and play a single melody.
Is there anyone? After a long silence, he said: "The poor have no noble man to offer gold; the sick have only idle people to prescribe medicinal formulas."
When Master Kuān arrived, the Master drew this circle and gave it to Kuān, then went out himself to perform manual labor.
The next day, he ascended the hall and asked Kuān before the Dharma seat, "How did you handle yesterday's public case? Kuān [responded] upon the ground.
Having drawn this circle with the "ox" [symbol] inside, he rubbed it away with his foot. The Master then said, "The title of Chan-head Kuān is not obtained in vain.
He then ascended the seat and said: "Suddenly, the sound of a thunderclap in a clear sky; The waves of the Three Cascades at Yumen roar and crash.
How many with heads and horns have gone forth as dragons? Shrimp and crabs still glare with their eyes as before."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To forge a hook from a needle—how could this be a sound plan? Only by cutting across the sea with a vast net does one act as a true master.

When suddenly encountering a scaled dragon with crimson tail, one must cause its whiskers to shake the void. But as for the lame tortoise and the blind turtle, let them go their own way in groups of three or two.
Why is this so? Having once been a wandering gambler, I am especially fond of guests; I myself love to cherish the cup."
"Pity the Drunken Man.

He ascended the hall and said: "To awaken to the Way by hearing sounds is no different from climbing a tree to seek fish. To clarify the mind by seeing forms is much like losing one's head and recognizing only its reflection.
You people of virtue, there is no need to shorten the crane to match the duck, or to level the mountains to fill the valleys. [Look at] the Southern Dipper and the Northern Dipper."

The celestial mansions and degrees are clearly defined; the sun is obscured while the moon shines bright, their rising and sinking naturally distinct. I simply ask that you cease military expeditions and lay down arms, remaining upright and non-active (*wuwei*).
Then, you will naturally find the point of entry and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If you further speak of discerning the meaning within words or clarifying the pivot within phrases, you are like a man waiting by a tree stump under the clear breeze and moonlight—the cool rabbit has long since fled and the spring grasses grow green.

Ascending the hall, he said: "One is not released, two are not gathered; the herdsman plays his flute crosswise while riding backward on the ox. In the pine bower, the moon is cold and the dream has just been broken.
A single sound blows forth the autumn at the frontier gates."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The autumn wind blows briskly; the autumn rain falls gently. The guest geese have not yet arrived;

the sea swallows are about to return. The cicadas chirp as the forest thins and the leaves fall; the moon shines bright as tigers roar and monkeys wail. Whether heard or seen, who is enlightened and who is deluded?
Whether you understand or not, do not confuse the needle with the awl. Do you not see? The old woman of Xinfeng stands alone in peril."
Not a blade of grass grows for thousands of miles; yet upon stepping out the door, what is it that spreads so luxuriantly?
He ascended the hall and said: "Bodhisattvas crave merit; Śrāvakas stagnate in stillness. The multitudes of sentient beings within the three realms do not recognize the power of this grace.
Therefore, I pray you turn the light back and let the mind-consciousness rest. When a single thought accords with reality, the profound pivot may be struck."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In all directions, there is a vast clamor of debate; at Fachang, it is cool and sparse.

Let the ancient halls be allowed to grow moss, so as to avoid filling the ditches and blocking the ravines. To flaunt divine mechanisms and boast of subtle strategies—when calculated, these are all merely idle deliberations."
How can it compare to tearing asunder the great void? Realize that one stroke of the Tathāgata! *Ai!* Mistake! Entering the hall, he said:
"The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. He raised his staff and said:
"Śākyamuni has transformed himself into this single staff, now in the hands of Fachang. When it is raised..."
He cuts off the three vehicles. To let go is to levelly deceive the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Suddenly encountering a bewildered Chan practitioner, Fachang hurriedly steps back. After a long silence, he says: "Look!"
On the first day of the year, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the lingering cold of the first month of spring;

does the Dharma exist at the beginning of the New Year? The Master said, "The eastern mountains and western ridges are green. The monk pressed further, "This is still worldly dharma; what is the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Rarely does one encounter a guest with pierced ears; most are but men who mark the water's edge. The monk pressed further, "What can be done about this student?"
[The monk] did not understand. The Master said, "Even when presented face-to-face, you still do not understand; it would be better to recite 'Svāhā' in a quiet place. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "A sharp and clever patch-robed monk. A monk asked, "The new year has already passed;
I wonder what is the phrase regarding that which does not migrate? The Master said, "Where it was once broken last year, today it grows branches again. [The monk] further asked, "This..."
"This is the persistence of that which has passed away. The Master said, "Things arise following people. The monk asked, "I wonder, is the patriarch’s nostril new or old?
The Master said, "Where did you see the patriarch? The monk replied, "I fear, Master, that I am not being truthful.
The Master said, "Tell me then, is it new or old? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "You failed even to ask about the error."

The Master then said: "The four seasons revolve in a cycle, ending and beginning again. A hundred years of time pass as swiftly as snapping one's fingers. To beat the drum and ascend the hall is the custom of all quarters;

yet when the vehicle of the ultimate teaching is raised for discussion, errors and disputes arise like swarms of bees. When conditions gather, there is birth; when conditions disperse, there is death.
As long as one has not escaped saṃsāra, how can one evade it? Enough, enough! When the time comes to act, act; when the time comes to rest, rest."
Stop! Do you not see? When Bodhidharma first arrived in the Wei dynasty, he had his front teeth knocked out by someone.
He then ascended the hall and said: "The void and clarity illuminate themselves; there is no need for mental effort.

If one can understand it here, then please cast away the pearls and discard the jade, cease battle and lay down arms. Not only will the Way flourish and times be peaceful, but the state and its people will also enjoy tranquility. Why?
Above is heaven; below is earth. The sun revolves within the void. Even if a jade pool were as clear as a mirror, it would ultimately make it difficult for the bright moon to descend.
If the profound mechanism remains concealed and the dark operation still lies dormant, then even one with six arms and three heads must still offer up the sheep and present the jade璧 (bi).
Ascending the hall, he said: "Do not, do not! Great men, why such great error? The clay ox knows only how to drive the vehicle of the school;
the wooden horse has never grown calf-horns. The fish does not roost, the bird does not nest. For the heavens of Liao, one must have the crane of Liao.
Knowing only how to commit grave offenses that obstruct Bodhi, they fail to realize the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. Enough, enough! Do not grope about. This is the Supreme Amṛta."
Flavors are treasures cherished by the world; when encountered by such people as these, they become poisonous medicine.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally. I do not ask about the petals—what is the flower? The Master said:
"Lush blossoms reach to the heavens in their elegance; fragrant scents spread across the earth in their crimson. The monk pressed further: "What kind of ground is this?"
[The Master] planted it. The Master said, "It grows from the rain of Vulture Peak; it blossoms because of the wind of Shaoshi. The student asked, "I wonder when it will bear fruit?
The Master said, "As long as the root and trunk are sound, why worry that the fruit will not be harvested? The student asked, "Does the student have a share in this or not?
The Master said, "There is no share. The student asked, "Everyone is fully endowed with it; why does the student have no share?"
The Master said: "Do not bring the eyes of the mundane realm into this garden of awakening.
He then continued: "Yesterday I gazed upon the flowers in the courtyard; today I enjoy the fragrant grasses. The fragrant grasses and the courtyard flowers each vie with one another for their beauty.
Yet the flowers wither before the grasses do, and the grasses likewise wither along with the flowers. How is it that people of this floating world do not awaken?"
Life is difficult to preserve. After a long silence, he said: "Why wait for things to wither and fall before one finally realizes they are empty?
He ascended the hall and said: "The dragon roars and the mist rises; the tiger howls and the wind arises. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*), not produced by artificial effort.

Those superior practitioners who investigate the profound must skillfully discern the appropriate occasion; do not rely on another's gate or eat another's leftover rice. Furthermore, this is your own matter."
The matter is, right here, clearly manifest. Its application is boundless; it is not obtained from others. It has no inherent rank or position—do not force it into a framework.
This brilliant spiritual light transcends all measure and number. Following conditions, it is expansive and free; according to its nature, it floats or sinks.

Like the bright sun in the sky, like a lotus emerging from the water, it is unfathomable to both sages and ordinary beings; how could it be categorized among mundane things? Furthermore, do not seek it within words.
Then, applying ink and vermilion beneath the words is much like painting a cake to satisfy hunger; in the end, it provides no benefit. He ascended the hall and said:
"To awaken to the Way upon hearing sound, and to clarify the mind upon seeing form. He then picked up his staff and said, "Is this not 'seeing'?
He struck the meditation seat once and said, "Is this not 'hearing'? Which of these is the matter of awakening? If you say...
To hear a sound and think it is "I," or to see a form and think it is "another"—yellow-mouthed infants nodding their heads and swallowing their own saliva;
this was but a scene of shame before the Many-Sons Stūpa. Why is it so? Who knows that beyond the distant misty waves there is yet another way of thinking?
Ascending the hall, he said: "On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the Mid-Autumn Festival, the dew washes the layered cliffs until their light is pure and bright.

At every place, the pearl curtains are rolled back to reveal the clear radiance; one does not know that it is merely the moon of old. O worthy ones, as for the matter of each person’s own self, it is wondrous beyond words.
It cannot be recognized by consciousness, nor can it be known by intellect. The entire body of the temporal teachings is but a mere footnote."
By means of the Way and the Sūtra teachings, they are like a finger pointing at the moon. You brother-disciples who study together: having arrived here, what should you do?
Since the entire Tripitaka is but a pointing finger, tell me, where is the moon? Have you not seen how a monk asked Touzi:
"The Vulture Peak is like a finger pointing at the moon; Caoxi is like a painting of the moon. What is the true moon? Touzi said: [The moon is right here.]
Last night at the third watch, he turned toward the west. Touzi the Ancient Buddha was well-versed in the timing of the occasion;
like a bell on its stand, it emits sound according to the strike; like a mirror upon its pedestal, it reflects whatever comes before it.

Yet, such was his provisional expedient that this monk, having barely escaped the wind and thunder, was struck by a bolt of lightning once more. How could this compare to Fachang, who directly told him the truth right then and there? Thereupon—
Having finished drawing the circle, he said: "This night, the single orb is full; where is its pure light not present?
He then ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'As for the person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, though they have gained entry, it is not yet the ultimate reality.'"
"One must advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one manifests the entire body.

But how does one advance from the top of a hundred-foot pole? Do you wish to understand? In Jambudvīpa to the south and Uttarakuru to the north, one may walk when one wishes to walk and rest when one wishes to rest.
Yet, if you should suddenly encounter Xuansha, he will strike you until your head is split and your brain is shattered. Tell me, what is there [to it]?
[The Master] said, "It is past. "The eyes on the tip of the staff are as bright as the sun; one must recognize true gold by looking at it in the fire. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the four mountains press in from all sides? The Master said, "The precious carriage is outside the gate. The monk stepped forward and asked further.
"Does the Master have no skillful means? The Master said, "Chasing after life and pursuing pleasure in trivial pursuits—when called back, they do not turn their heads;
what can be done? The monk asked further, "What if they were suddenly called back? The Master said, "If you simply prepare a heart of resolve, I shall certainly not deceive you.
The monk asked, "A master of the school! The Master said, "This too is finding life within death. As the monk hesitated, the Master [struck him].
He struck him. The Master then said: "There are countless dead people on level ground. Those who can pass through the thorn forest are true adepts.

They do not prize their own spirits, nor do they seek after the sages. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, they do not rely upon a single thing; this is precisely what is meant by 'level ground.'"
The matter lies here: if you give rise to a thought or stir a念 (nien), you immediately deviate from the essence of the Dharma.

Furthermore, when the Great Function manifests, one displays jeweled king-lands upon the tip of a hair and turns the Great Wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust; yet this is called "wetting the bed while wide awake."
"It does not require a single shout from this old monk. But tell me, how does one penetrate a thicket of brambles? After a long silence, he said:
"Carry your poems and books back to your former retreat; wild flowers and singing birds are all part of the same spring."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the three realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four elements are fundamentally empty;
upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell? O spiritually sharp ones! As soon as you hear this being raised, you should cut off both ends and return home to sit in peace.
Let the monasteries be vast and the communities crowded—how joyful that would be! Yet do not take this lightly. Suddenly, if there were a man who came forth..."
"Come, clap your hands once. Do you hear it? Raise up this whisk. Do you see it? This is a magnificent 'Dharma-less-ness.
[The Master] strikes him a blow across the spine and prods him with a needle through his nostrils, waiting for you to recognize pain and discern itchiness. This is a magnificent 'Buddha-less-ness.
At this very moment, do not say that Fachang has misled you. Do you understand? Do not let the bright day pass in vain; the spring youth..."
"No more coming.
He ascended the hall and, picking up his staff, said: "If I pick it up, you call it 'first illumination, then function.
If I set it down, you call it 'first function, then illumination. If I throw it down, you call it 'illumination'."
At that very moment, suddenly neither grasping nor releasing—where would you go to speculate?

Even if you were to understand this with such clarity and decisiveness, should you encounter Linji or Deshan, you would quickly find your forehead hitting the ground. Tell me, what excellence does he possess?
After a long silence, he said: "Having experienced the great ocean, do not boast of its waters; apart from Mount Sumeru, there is nothing."

Shan ascended the hall and said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth. If you wish to attain manifestation before you, do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance.
O worthy ones, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth clearly manifest the host and guest; the sages and worthies of the three realms reflect one another’s radiance. Upon reaching this point—"
Inwardly, he does not grasp at a single dharma, nor does he discard a single dharma; furthermore, there is no cognition or understanding of grasping or discarding.
This is called the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi). It is precisely the sweat-shirt that clings to one’s skin. Thus, without abandoning the Way-dharma, he manifests all dignified deportments;

he vanishes within a spark from a flint and emerges within a flash of lightning. Through the "ladder of knives" and the "tree of swords," through tiger dens and demon palaces, he passes with unimpeded mastery in every direction.
Each and every detail is clearly manifest. Let me ask you this: upon the tips of the hundred grasses, have you ever seen Jia Shan in a dream?
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I do not ask about the meaning of the Patriarchs' coming from the West; but what of the matter of the trees shedding their leaves? The Master said:
The entire style of the Shaoshi tradition is fully revealed; how could you, O Acharya, fail to be alert? The monk asked, "What can be done about its withering away?
The Master said, "The mountains' shadows shift before the eyes. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how should one understand this?
The Master said, "If one is not a true connoisseur, it is all in vain to speak of the severity of winter. A monk asked, "The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words."
"How does the school of Shaoshi proclaim its teaching? The Master said, "When one house has business, a hundred houses are busy.
The monk asked, "This is still a point of doubt for a student. The Master said, "If you are a phoenix chick, you do not scurry about the fence. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "I do not yet believe you. He then continued: "The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, there is indeed profound mystery.
If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow. You worthy ones, look! Look!
Śākyamuni, donning fur and wearing horns, climbs mountains of knives and enters masses of fire, and then transforms himself into a water buffalo."
"He has run off into the ranks of Mt. Huishan! Do you all see him? If you see him, I grant you one eye;
if you do not see him, I also grant you one eye. But tell me, where is Fachang’s eye for guiding others?
After a long silence, he said: "Do not inscribe names upon fallen leaves, lest they be carried away by the flowing stream."

Arriving at the human realm, he ascended the hall and said: "This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; there is no further sound or form to present to you. If one understands this point, there is nothing at all;
essence and function do not hinder one another, whether they are divided or not. The cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies—every phenomenon is perfectly complete. Water...
The green mountains are verdant; every aspect is manifest and brilliant. Seeing is the same as seeing; hearing is the same as hearing. For what reason, then, are there delusion and enlightenment?
After a long silence, he said: "Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is nothing much; it is not known by those who have not undergone diligent effort."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one is a person who 'knows there is,' entering the forest they do not stir the grass; entering the water they do not stir the waves.
They are then able to cast off their precious and noble robes and don tattered, soiled garments. Joining hands with the various demons, they act as companions among the weary.

Welcoming those who come from all quarters—this is still merely a matter of borrowing from the periphery. Why? Even when the source is clear and the waters still, they still row a solitary boat. Ancient...

The Buddha’s place of enlightenment is like riding in a carriage. If you are one of those within this circle, you must simply scratch an itch on the head of a serpent, pluck the pearl from beneath the jaw of a black dragon, drive away the oxen of the plowman, and snatch the food from a starving man.

If you can do such things, only then will you understand how to sit upon the heads of the response and transformation Buddhas and tread upon the crown of Vairocana. When Fachang speaks in this manner, it is much like speaking in a dream.
A Dream. What does this mean? It is like neither coming nor going; there is neither laughter nor sorrow.
[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks: "From Buddha to Buddha the hand is passed, from patriarch to patriarch it is transmitted. I wonder, what is it that is transmitted? The Master says:
[The student asked: "Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru is the Iron Kunlun. What does this signify? The Master said: "Leaving one's country, one knows the way home;
wandering in solitude, one obtains the precious pearl. [The student] asked: "In the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust can remain.
Where, then, is this pearl placed? The Master said: "From the beginning, it has been brilliantly radiant; there is no need for forced arrangement. [The student] said: "If that is so..."
The monk then thanked the Master for his instruction. The Master asked, "Where is the pearl? The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Finished. The Master then continued:

"Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-organ are removed, the dust of the world vanishes and awareness becomes perfectly pure.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, it encompasses all of space. Returning then to observe the world, it is as if..."
This is a matter of dreams. O worthy ones, the gateway of the Patriarchs has already been flung wide open by the Old Man Śākyamuni;
there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation. To realize this directly may be called outshining the past and excelling the future.
If you still have further deliberations, then I shall grant that you possess a single eye.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The *maṇi* jewel is not recognized by people; it is personally held within the *tathāgatagarbha*. What is this jewel? The Master said:
"There is no place to seek it in the Dragon Palace; how could the oceanic treasury contain it? The monk further asked:
"I do not yet understand where it ultimately resides. The Master drew a circle. The monk opened both hands. The Master struck him. The monk bowed. The Master said: "Three."
That may still be tolerable; but when day breaks, it brings even more sorrow to people.

The Master then said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons.
As the four seasons revolve, the myriad phenomena flourish; yet seeing and hearing are not obscured—the powers of sight and sound remain distinct. Furthermore:
"Which of these is the master? Is it this one who comes in such a manner? Is it this wondrous essence that has fundamentally no location?
Is it this totality when not a single thought has yet arisen?
To speculate in this way is much like sitting in a well to gaze at the sky, or peering through a tube to view a leopard. For one who is truly authentic, none of this toil is necessary.
“Suffering! After a long silence, he said: “In the narrow alleys, one does not ride a golden horse; returning, one puts on a tattered robe.
On the festival day, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: “The ancients said, ‘When the yang energy arises, there is no hard ground.
Why does the rootless tree not bloom? The Master said: “You do not even look after the head of the phrase. The monk pressed further: “But what can be done?”
A monk was fully prepared. The Master asked, "Where is your tree standing? The monk lifted up his sitting mat. The Master said, "You are mocking this old fellow," and struck him.
A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Patriarch’s intent coming from the West; as for the matter of directly pointing to the source, what is it?
The Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. The Master gave another shout and clapped his hands once. The monk said, "A master of the school."
The Master said, "A note! The monk bowed. The Master said, "Before you have even stepped onto the stage, you are already extraordinary.

The Master then continued: "The first yang returns, and all things know spring. By the embankment, the eyes of the willows vie to open; by the mountain stream, the petals of the plum blossoms compete to burst forth.
On the crags, the trees are frozen; where can the vermilion phoenix perch? In the abyss, the moon is locked in ice; the roaming dragon has not yet stirred. The brocade..."
The young master is dressed in fine robes, utterly intoxicated like mud. The man of the Way beneath the forest trees covers his head and sleeps.
Do not sleep! Leisurely gaze at the flowing waters by the riverhead. Fine things in this world are not enduring; colorful clouds easily disperse, and lapis lazuli is fragile.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The difficulty of the journey—look for it yourself! The bird-path has never been easy to ascend. Before the traveler even begins the climb, they must stoop;
Their chin and knees frequently touch one another. Only by clutching at the vines to reach the very summit Does one finally realize that the world is vast and empty."
Ascending the hall, he said: The flowers are fragrant; the rain falls fine. Travelers upon the road are like mud.
Who is it in the painted tower blowing the jade flute? With every single note, the sun is sent sinking in the west.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it simply dislikes discrimination. The sages and ordinary people of the three realms are like mud and water mixed together;
the lanterns and the pillars are blunt and indistinct. As for the birth-and-death of ordinary beings and the nirvana of the Buddhas—how can one attain non-discrimination?
Is it not the case that a difference of a hair's breadth makes heaven and earth as far apart? Or is it realized when emotions are exhausted and perfect clarity is attained?"

Take it as such. Is this not the principle that "the myriad dharmas are but consciousness" and that "all is my own mind"? There can be no further distinction between self and other; let us rejoice that there is no connection [to be made].
If it were Fa-chang, he would say: "Right is right, and wrong is wrong. The sun is warm in the southland, and the partridges cry."
Neither non-being nor being, neither is nor not-is—this turns one’s laughter at Vimalakīrti’s discourse on non-duality.
If you have not yet penetrated the profound mystery herein, for now, realize the Tathāgata’s primary truth.

On an evening small assembly during the summer retreat, he said: "Generally speaking, you brothers who have come to study the Way, as long as your vision of the Path is not yet clear and your mind-ground is not yet at peace, whenever you enter a monastic grove or leave a community, you must associate closely with virtuous friends and good companions.

Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night, you must take the Buddha-Dharma as your primary concern and resolutely investigate it until your heart-mind becomes sharp and brilliant. This is no small matter."
Matters are such that time and light are easily lost; the moment does not wait for man. Once one has lost this human body, there will ultimately be no way out.

Do not merely spend your time in such idle clamor, saying "today the third, tomorrow the fourth," passing the winter here and the summer there, carrying a bellyful of tangled vines and scholarly interpretations in your mind, and everywhere plundering the void, smoothing your lips and stroking your beak.
Speaking Chinese and barbarian tongues alike, you claim to understand Chan and understand the Way, yet you treat good people with contempt and commit the karma of the Avīci Hell.
You should know that this matter is not at all easy. Even men of immeasurable stature find no place to set their heads or noses here;
do not take it lightly and open your big mouths recklessly. Old man Fachang has no human sentiment and does not love people; he merely rubs and pats you to praise you.

I lament you. All of this is not out of good intent. One day, when fire and wind disperse and the light of the eyes falls to the ground, the karmic conditions of good and evil, the retribution of the beautiful and the ugly, and the realms of birth and death will all manifest at once.
At that time, you will be like a crab falling into boiling water—your hands flailing and your feet scrambling;

Reaching this point, it is truly like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night. Yet even these are matters belonging to the shore of birth and death. Do not..."
Do not take this lightly; you must not fail to see the Way of the ancients.

You must first shoulder the burden over there, and only then return here to pack your gear, polish your mind and consciousness, and exhaust all present-day afflictions until you are like a withered tree encountering spring—yet remaining without moisture.
Only then will there be a slight degree of accord. When the ancients spoke in such a manner, what was their intention?
What is being carried on that side? And how is one’s baggage managed on this side? Unless one has long studied under a master of great virtue, one cannot know this.
Do not merely remain thus, with your consciousness busily preoccupied by ignorance, egoism, and private interpretations, vainly creating conceptual fabrications.
"Carving [the mirror]—it is like polishing a brick to make a mirror. There is much error here; you must apply yourself with vigor.
Do not wait until the path ahead is exhausted before you begin to be anxious. Once your mind’s eye suddenly opens, you will finally know that Old Facha took the Buddha-dharma as his sole task."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Yesterday we saw off the old year; this morning we celebrate the new year. The new year and the old year pursue one another like flowing water.
There is no person who lives for a hundred years; all but create a thousand-year burden. This single impermanent body gives rise to a hundred schemes:
it kills living beings to satisfy the mouth and belly, and commits karma in pursuit of wealth and status. Not a single fragment of goodness has ever been cultivated. Day after day...
Intoxicated by afflictions? Do not be intoxicated! Arise and let me speak with you for a moment.

From the Zhou, Qin, Han, and Wei dynasties—those who established hegemonies and plotted for kingship, whose civil strategies were as warp and martial prowess as woof—their names fill the Lingyan Pavilion like hemp seeds. Yet they all lie prostrate, sleeping beneath the feet of the green mountains.
How can they compare to the gate of non-action and true reality, where one transcends directly and enters the stage of the Tathāgata?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Every year on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, everywhere else observes the *jinzu* (the retreat). But how is it here within the mountains of Fachang?
One simply sees the mountains green and the waters clear."
Ascending the hall, he said: "O worthy ones, the mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like stains upon a mirror. When the stains and grime are exhausted, the light finally appears.
When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, the nature is itself true. The ancients have already set their four corners firmly upon the ground.
How do you all understand this? Looking inward, one does not see oneself; turning back to listen, one does not hear the self."

I have heard that the essence of awakening is transcendent and does not belong to numerical measure; it is precisely these traces and defilements that reside within you. Now tell me, where is the mirror?
Even if you were to clearly bring it forth, I would further ask you: from where did you obtain it?
If you do not know its place of origin, I, this mountain monk, shall point it out for you: "The copper mountains have been smelted until not a single star remains; it has entered the red furnace."
Furthermore, regarding "dust," one must know that things are fundamentally and spontaneously perfected; being fundamentally and spontaneously perfected, they are without old or new.
When the Master was at Shuangling, having accepted an invitation, he took his leave of the two head seats, Ying and Sheng, saying: "We have been together for three years. No [further words].
“I do not understand this matter. Examining it closely, there is no lack of leakage. [The Master] struck a line with his staff and said, “Let this matter rest for now;
as for the matter of the Zen school, what is it? Ying said, “Mount Sumeru fits into the nostrils.

The Master said, “If that is so, then looking at a tiger’s eyes from the edge of a cliff, one needlessly falls into a fit of sorrow. Ying said, “Deep-Sand (the Nāga) bulges his eyes. The Master said, “How can you compare them?”
"Indeed, there is no different path for the sage and the ordinary person; yet there are many gates to skillful means. Ying said, "An iron snake cannot be pierced by a drill.
The Master said, "What common ground is there for conversation with such a fellow? Ying said, "It is simply because my own faculties are shallow; do not resent the springtime of the Great Sun."
He then made a single stroke with his staff and said, "Let us set aside the affairs of the Zen school for a moment; as for this matter, how is it? The Master then struck him.
Yingshan said, "You man from Zhangzhou, do you have no sense of propriety? The Master said, "With a view such as yours, when would I wait to strike you?
He struck him again. Yingshan said, "This too was brought upon me by the old monk."
Xuefeng and Yingsheng went together to visit the mountain. Yingsheng said, "The Master usually likes to examine and critique those from all quarters;
why is it that today you have instead come to make a living inside an old temple? The Master said, "I am merely striking the grass so as to startle the snake.
Yingsheng said, "Do not try to deceive people like this. The Master said, "And what are you doing thrusting your head into a vat of glue? Yingsheng... [remained silent].
[Yun] said, "The ancients said, 'I see two clay oxen fighting their way into the sea,' and that is why I dwell in the mountains. But I wonder, Master, what do you see?
The Master said, "When you reach another day in the future, and someone comes to ask you while you are covering your head with a handful of thatch—how will you respond?
Ying said, "The summit of the mountain is not as good as the foot of the ridge. The Master said, "But tell me first—"
“Can one truly dwell in the affairs of the mountain? Yingshan said, “The spade is not as good as the plow. The Master said, “Have you ever dreamed of the ancients?
Yingshan said, “And what about you, Master? The Master spread his two hands. Yingshan said, “A shrimp cannot leap out of its bucket.
The Master said, “Do not take a three-inch candle and try to rival the brilliance of the sun. Yingshan said, “What can be done about this public case?”
[The Master] was present. He said, "The Chan practitioners are as numerous as hemp and millet.
The Master rose from the Dharma Hall and asked the two men, "I wish to build a Dharma Hall here; tell me, what function does it serve?
Ying said, "The thief is the petty man. The Master said, "Zi of Shaowu, you act as soon as you are provoked."
Feces have a foul odor. Yanguan said, "I have once suffered the bitterness of frost and snow. The Master said, "A bright pearl naturally has a price of a thousand pieces of gold;
who would be willing to beat a sparrow by the woods? Yanguan said, "It is very much like holding an alms bowl and falsely claiming one is not hungry.
The Master then pointed at Sheng and said, "Tell me, what kind of response would you offer? Sheng said, "The original nature."
"There is no fixed position; there is no need for forced arrangement. The Master said, "Where would you place this donkey-man?
Sheng said, "I leave it to you to beat the bricks and smash the tiles. The Master said, "He is merely a fabricated magistrate.

Ying said, "If it were a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, why would one need to strike at a sparrow? The Master said, "When a member of the eastern family dies, the western family offers its condolences. Ying...
It is said: "When one sees injustice on the road, one must rectify it.
One day, Xuefeng brought up the kōan concerning Daming’s cutting off of the debate between Jiangshan and Dingshan regarding whether there is a Buddha within birth-and-death or not.
He asked the Master, "How would you handle this case? The Master said, "Why did Daming not [cut them off] at that time?"
Regarding the "grass and fodder" of one's own portion, Xuefeng said, "How is it? Yunyan then struck him. Yunyan said, "A total mess.

[The Master] brought up the story of Panshan Guangjing. Ying said, "As for Baofu speaking in such a manner, he cannot avoid being on people's lips and teeth.
The Master asked, "What do you say? Ying made a gesture of slapping with his palm. The Master said, "You do not even know the stench of your own excrement.
Ying asked, "How about you, Preceptor? The Master said, "According to my own view, I would dig a pit in the ground and bury you both in it."
At that time, [the master] buried it away, wishing only for peace throughout the world.
Layman Huanglong Xiu and several monks arrived. The Master said, "The mountain passes and roads are layered upon one another;
from where have you come, Ācārya? Xiu replied, "I have come from within the main gate. The Master said, "If there is a main gate, then you must have come from within the main gate."
"Since there are no three gates, from where do they come? Xiu said, "In that case, they do not enter through the gate.
The Master said, "By what means have you arrived here? Xiu said, "At Fa-chang’s gate, the water flows out and cannot be blocked.

The Master said, "You do not know how to climb the mountain, yet you stubbornly complain that the path is winding. As Xiu hesitated, the Master said, "The second head monk, speak! The monk said, "What?"

Once the social formalities were concluded, Xiu said, "The case just now could truly be called 'illuminating the past and surpassing the future.

"This is the principle. The Master then asked Xiu, "Where have you recently come from? Xiu replied, "Huanglong. The Master said, "I have heard that Huanglong has three 'gateless barriers' (san guan);

There was an answer. The Master said, "Before you have reached Fachang, it is not without reason that you harbor doubts. Xiu asked, "Where does the fault lie?
The Master struck him with his palm and said, "Do not be so dull-witted as Huanglong.
He then escorted him back to his quarters. Xiu said, "The ancients said, 'If one word accords, one stays; if one word does not accord, one leaves. Now tell me: would staying be right, or leaving?"
The Master said, "Look! This fellow has met with a total defeat. Xiu said, "In that case, the army follows the seal, and the guest is subject to the host's judgment.

The Master said: "A divine colt from a thousand miles away chases the lightning; the lame donkey still sinks into the mud.
One day Xiu asked the Master, "I have heard that you, Reverend, stayed at Fushan for a long time and frequently visited Xinghua.

Xiu replied, "This old fellow does not even know his own defeat. The Master said, [and remained silent].

The Master was discussing with Nan the Chan Master the story of Cheng Daxiang looking at his "birth affinity" (*shengyuan*).

The rain falls heavily; clouds enshroud the moon as the tide’s sound rises. It seems there is no intent to suppress the surrounding peaks, yet there remains a constant heart that yearns for the falling snow.
Monkeys, frozen, descend the cliffs and wail as they climb back up; after meditation, I stand alone, chanting amidst the bitterness.

Kuān replied, "I am merely passing through for a short time. The Master asked, "Where was Maitreya Bodhisattva when you came?
Kuān replied, "I do not know. The Master asked, "Did the Abbot come from Tuṣita? Kuān replied, "Yes. The Master asked, "Why?"
Yet he did not know. Kuān said, "I told you from the start that you do not know. Why speak of coming or not coming? The Master said, "A holeless iron hammer—what use is it?
Kuān said, "Watch this old fellow; what a display of confusion! Once, while the Master and National Teacher Kuān were looking at the snow, the Master said, "Beautiful snow.
Kuān said, "Beautiful white. The Master said, "Between snow and white, how much difference is there?"
Guang said, "It is like making a fist from an open palm. The Master then grabbed some snow on the railing and struck him, saying, "Now tell me, is this a fist or a palm?

There is a poem that says: Leaning on the railing, I watch the winter snow; Its light pierces the cold of the dawn hall. The ocean of Mañjuśrī’s myriad virtues— A thousandfold [layers]...

The world is vast; the shadows and light of the clay ox are in disarray. The stone woman’s white robe remains intact. If you understand the meaning of youth, it will be even more difficult to awaken amidst the peach blossoms.

"Flavor. What is it like? Huanglong said, "One must wait until one has tasted it before one can know.
The Master said, "To test a person at the point of certainty, one knows them the moment they take a bite. Huanglong said, "Cen masters of this degenerate age are mostly empty and seldom substantial.
The Master again picked up the bowl and asked, "How do you taste this? Huanglong said, "It must be the Master himself who tastes it. The Master said, "One..."
This fellow is already beyond help. Ganyun said, "To forgive others is not the mark of a weak man.
The Master asked Chief Seat Ne: "The ancients said, 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me.'"
"Tell me, are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as your own self, or are they different? Nan said, "They are not different.
The Master then held up his whisk and said, "What about this? Nan said, "This is also so. The Master asked, "How many selves do you have?
Nan said, "Phenomena (*dharma*) are manifold, but the principle (*li*) is fundamentally non-dual. The Master then struck the meditation bench once and said:
"Do you still know pain and itchiness? Nan said, "I do not. The Master said, "The talk has slipped away; this master cannot beat you.
One day, while the Master was with the Head Seat Nan repairing a flower altar, he asked Nan, "Nanquan said, 'Everyone sees...'"
“This single flower is like a dream. Tell me, what do you see that is like this? Nan said, “It is just a single flower.
The Master said, “If that is so, then you remain within the nest of Nanquan. Nan asked, “I wonder, what was the meaning of the ancients?
The Master said, “Bring me a brick. After Nan had brought the brick, he asked again. The Master—
[The Master] said: "The ancients have long since passed away.
He asked Elder Huo, "I hear it is said that you once lectured on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; is this true? Huo replied, "I have studied and listened to it roughly."
The Master said, “The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. He stated this principle clearly. Huo said, “Yes.
The Master then held up his whisk and asked, “Do you see it? Huo said, “I see it. The Master asked, “What do you see? Huo said, “I see the whisk. The Master said, “You are old and venerable;
why is it that you do not observe the five precepts? Huo said, “How can you, Reverend, [speak thus]?”
[The monk] did not believe the Master’s words. The Master said, "Foolish man, you cannot die even if struck with a staff. Do you still dream of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)?
The Master asked the Venerable Zhao, "Where have you come from? Zhao said, "I have come to fetch vegetables. The Master said, "Where are you going? Zhao said, [he was going to the latrine].
The Master went into the quarters. He said, "I usually ask you about the matter of life and death; why do you not respond in this way?
Zhao said, "The Master has never asked me. The Master said, "Tell me then, where will you go when you die?"
Zhao said, "I leave it entirely to your conjecture. The Master said, "I do not believe you. Zhao said, "In my responding to you in this way, what is there that is not acceptable?
The Master said, "I thought you were incapable of such conjecture. Zhao said, "But tell me, where does it go?"
The Master said, "He has gone into the ghost cave. Zhaor said, "Do not obstruct others with your own self. The Master said, "What can you do?
The stolen goods are in my hands."
[The Master] asked Huizhao: "When the sun rises, the light of the mind shines; when the sky is overcast, the nature-ground is dark.

For one who does not know heaven and earth, the Way of Firmness possesses the Qian and Kun hexagrams. But now that the sun has risen, which of these is the light of your mind? Huizhao said: "It cannot be anything else. The Master said:
"For one who does not know heaven and earth, the Way of Firmness possesses the Qian and Kun hexagrams. Now tell me, for one who *does* know heaven and earth—where do Qian and Kun abide?"
"Where has it gone? Zhao said, "The three realms are mind-only; there can be nothing else.
The Master said, "When you light a fire in the kitchen, do you feel your belly grow hot? Zhao asked, "Why ask about this? The Master said, "You dead-end Zen monks!"
