The Master said: "Paper is in high demand in Tanzhou; one document suffices for all.
The Master visited the Hermitage Master of Bājiā Quán and asked, "Is the Hermitage Master at home? Quán asked, "Who is it? The Master said, "A traveling monk.
Quán asked, "What brings you here? The Master said, "To pay my respects to the Hermitage Master. Quán said, "It happens that I have just met with the Hermitage Master's absence."
The Master said, "Are you there? Zhiquan replied, "I told you I am not here. Why speak of 'you' and 'me'? He grabbed his staff and chased him straight down the mountain.
The next morning he went again, and was chased away as before. Later, the Master went once more and asked, "Is the Hermitage Master there?
Zhiquan asked, "Who is it? The Master said, "A traveling monk. He pulled back the curtain and entered. Zhiquan blocked his way and seized him, saying, "There is a worm here!"
The tiger roams freely. This bed-wetting ghost has come three times and twice; what is he seeking? The Master said, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way.
Chuan then untied his robe and shook it out, saying, "You think there is something particularly extraordinary about me, Great Master Chuan.
The Master then asked, "Who is the master of this hermitage? Chuan said, "One must discern this upon entering the gate. The Master said, "Do not..."
"This very thing is it. Zhaozhou said, "How many people have been deceived! The Master said, "Where was your previous statement?
Zhaozhou said, "Listening to matters without clarity; calling a bell a jar. The Master said, "If that is so, then when the myriad dharmas are extinguished, the entire body is revealed.
Where the ruler and minister meet, the orthodox departs from the center. Zhaozhou said, "You blockhead! If you do not understand, then stop. Why do you speak such nonsense?"
Mou asked, "I do not know what you will use to receive a guest when he arrives. Quan said, "Yunmen’s fried cake and Zhaozhou’s tea.
The Master said, "If that is so, then I thank the Master for his hospitality. Quan said, "I have not even had my firewood prepared, yet you already speak of thanking me for my hospitality."
The Recorded Sayings of Fachang concludes.
Verses on Dongshan’s “Three Pounds of Flax.”
How shall we divide the seeds of the hemp? Brewed with last winter’s snow, this tea shall relieve your intoxication. Beyond lies a path no traveler has yet reached;
wild flowers smile, their old branches fresh with spring.
In the story of the wind and the banner, it is neither wind nor banner; it is a black flower-cat with a speckled face.
The traveler at night covets only the bright moon, unaware that his clothes are soaked by the cold water he has crossed.
Yunju is peaceful and happy;
the tree is peaceful and happy, walking alone in leisure. Striking the fifth watch at the third watch—how can one pass through this single thread? Flowing water mingles with the cry of the parrot;
the pavilion of congealed clouds.
Gathering clouds seal ten thousand folds; the towering peaks have level paths. How can one thread pass through? At midnight, the sun shines bright.
At Shuyuting, the "washing jade" is inherently flawless. Seeking it only makes it more distant. How can one thread pass through? Clouds and moon naturally veil it all.

At the Bridge over the Green Stream, the misty waves have stilled; myriad phenomena manifest within it, as if the same essence were being entrusted. A cold pine tree rises against the evening wind at the Dragon Pond.
The cold pond has no bottom or shore; deep within, a mud-dwelling dragon lurks. If you expose yourself to the vast empty sky, where will the traveler encounter you?
A general verse for five, four, three, two, and one: the Persian is as black as lacquer; having run past the source of Silla, the old woman mutters darkly in the shadows.
Dharmakāya Verse:
A snail swallows an elephant; a stone tiger bites a foreign horse. Startled, the dragon of the lineage breaks free; he tramples down the roof tiles of the cloud-house.
The price of rice in Luling.
The three-eyed tortoise is crimson; the auspicious qilin has a single sharp horn. As it soars through the clouds, evening rain arises; the mountain stream’s moon illuminates the night curtains.
As you, Secretary Lian, travel to Mount Zhurong, the waves at its peak surge on.
How many times have you circled the black-earth Sumeru? The hornless iron ox rests peacefully upon the tiger.
The distance: the jade maidens with their parted hair cross the Heavenly River. A-ha-ha! The bamboo staff strikes the void as the clouds rise high.

Presented to the Abbot of Shanshan Hermitage, who roams freely among groves and springs to nurture his pure leisure. A single expanse of level plain amidst the bright day—truly worthy for one to lodge the mind; who could attain this?
Companions! With smoke and vines, Han-shan withdraws his hand.
The fisherman has ceased casting his line;
the sun shines upon the green mountains as the accumulated snow melts away. The fisherman returns home to sing his own songs, letting others chase the waves and follow the currents.
At that time, he held a long pole and gazed toward the sea tide;

while reading the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, he realized through the "wondrous existence of bodhi" that there is no mind to be attained. He understood that original enlightenment contains all sentient beings, likened to a lotus amidst fire, and that true gold does not require the furnace.

Molten. In the void there are no flowers; the heavens blaze with crimson flames. Clouds rise from the precipitous cliffs as the spring drips and leaks; the wind blows through the cold leaves, which fall with a whirring sound.
If people of this age ask about True Perfect Enlightenment, when the thought of sleep arises, close your eyes and sleep.

Because of reading the scriptures—both the *Āgama* and *Nidāna* collections—one has fallen into a tangle. Looking closely, it is seen that this is a deliberate error. The old man from East Village beats Zhang San;
two benevolent deities both manifest their wrath. Do not manifest wrath! Last night, a cold monkey circled and wailed by the window; a white bird...
This morning I ascended the lofty pavilion;
seeing off a monk, I turned my staff upside down and struck the vast sky. Clouds arise as dragons race along the bird-path; with hands steady, I pull open the gate of the thousand sages.
The Eyes: In Jianghuai and Liangzhe, the scenery is fine from east to west.
Among these five poems on mountain dwelling, the pine-clad gate is quiet; I sleep soundly until midday before opening it. Who comes often to this scene? After the rain, white clouds arrive.

The birds, weary of their flight, pause at the rest-houses to call; the monkeys sit facing one another in pure meditation. The sound of the pines is cold and shrill; the mountain stream flows cool and thin.
I stroll idly through the shadows of the pines and encounter a man carrying firewood on his back. When I ask him where he is going, he says, "To the Ji River, white as silver."
In the landscape, pines support cranes; at home, there is no grain for hungry mice. When a guest arrives, what shall I offer? Only the medicinal herbs grow long in the mountain ravines.

The paths through the mountain gorges are steep and lofty; those who understand me have ceased their coming and going. How can I manifest a single token of faith? A stone shoot is fashioned from the clouds.

Beholding the mountains, the wind is swift and the floating clouds are hurried; the spring mountains turn green after the rain has passed. Let the traveler cease further questioning; the mountain stream resounds with a clear, cold murmur.
To bind oneself without a rope.

Clouds and cranes beyond the high heavens; forests and springs are by nature originally at ease. Why need one further seek out extraordinary places? It is like gouging out living flesh where it is not needed.
When the paper curtain is lifted in this verse, the whole body is revealed. Letting go, all subtle dust is extinguished. Who knows this meaning? Shide himself is filled with joy.
On account of this matter, Vajra opened the Buddha’s mouth; the Bodhisattva entered the gate of heaven. He took up his boots and garments and departed, concealing them in a place where no one dwelt.
A Verse on Cold Mountain (Hanshan). Dull and doltish; if one can recognize it, it is not on Mount Tiantai.

Entrusted to the new monks, this judgment has long been hidden deep within Dragon Peak. How many times have the peach blossoms bloomed? Looking at the mountain, is it seen or not? Not seeing it, one descends the mountain.
—The Verses on the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan song)
The Mystery within the Essence: A solitary-horned earthen ox sleeps upon the water; Turning its body, it strikes through the moon in the clear pool;
Atop Mount Wushan, waves surge to the heavens.
The Mystery within Function: A soldier in armor sleeps; Spring flowers are swept away by the wind; Yellow leaves fall before the steps.
The mystery within the phrase: remote from the Way, cut off from human smoke. A sweet melon is as sweet as honey; a bitter gourd is as bitter as a lotus.
The first phrase: a boundless mass of great fire. To hesitate is already to have one’s body turned to ash. Who dares to look directly at its head?
The second phrase: "The dragon soars and the tiger crouches; ask further of Vaiśālī, and you have already fallen onto another path.
The third phrase: "Cast off the mother-born trousers and directly take it up; an iron mountain lies across the road."
The First Secret: Three catties of iron within the sleeves. Suddenly encountering the sick Vimalakīrti, one seizes it up and strikes him right over the head.
The Second Secret: Snow covering the heavens in the sixth month. Nowhere to escape the scorching heat; the entire body is as cold as iron.
The Third Secret: Eight characters, not two; the Central Asian monk smiles and nods his head. Dust settles heavily upon his eyes.
At Fanchang’s Stone Mirror, neither ordinary nor sage is distinguished; all enter the perfect radiance, with nothing left behind.
At Fanchang’s Wooden Snake, claws are retracted and fangs hidden; if you suddenly bump into it, look beneath your feet.
Fachang’s iron staff stirs the wind and raises the waves; his playful spiritual powers serve as a model for all quarters.
At the song assembly, the head seat remained silent;
Mount Ou once again met guests from West Shu. Long may we sit together by the tall pines, beneath the high moonlight. Resting in peace.
The Meditation Rock: Sometimes it forgets its artifice, holding fast to subtle traces; sometimes it wanders free, haughty amidst the perilous azure. How towering and majestic is its verdant form!
Amidst layered islands of misty flowers, it laughs at the cold cypress. Like a straw dog barking upon the dewy ground, it strides forth with dignity into the Golden House.
A slender-waisted jade maiden rides upon it as a youth; when an old rustic encounters it, he pats it on its back. What is this? It is the thorn bush.
A mountain wall; two or three overturned painted jars. Following him as ants swarm toward the head, they crush his face with a horizontal slab of stone.
Sometimes following, sometimes opposing, the Persian does not fasten his waist-band.

He tramples over the eastern screen and the western fence, cleaving through the void to open a path for the Han traveler. Where light is clear and the dark ground is discerned, he laughs himself into oblivion at the village ahead.
Elder Zhang, do you remember those years when we sailed upon the iron boat? When it sank upon dry land, where could it be found? Sometimes bustling, sometimes silent;
through the vast expanse of past and present, morning and night are forgotten. My teacher, my teacher! The peach blossoms have fallen from their old fragrant branches.
To the traveler on the road, do not lend them out. Alas! Alas!
A verse on an occasion:
The lofty, verdant shadows of the Jasper Forest reflect in the clear depths of the pool. East Peak and West Pavilion, one, two, three. An iron ox lying in the water gallops toward the northern ridge;
a pair of crimson pillows are spread as the wild geese return to the south.
The bamboo grows lush because of the soil; the pines bend low as the clouds rise high. The setting sun illuminates empty shadows; a hungry mouse recites the name of Amitābha.
A fragment of water reflects the moon in the void; the pond is square, yet the water is not round. Mount Kunlun does not stare; the Vajra does not clench its fist.
The Master of Transmission has penetrated through;
a great man indeed, fiercely and boldly arrayed. Like a horned insect entering the marketplace, he need not conceal his sharp tongue when confronted by ups and downs.
Whenever he encounters the opportune moment, he strikes with swift ease, shattering the cave of Master Lu’s stinginess. The golden sun shines bright within his mouth.
In the center, the jade hare emerges; the orb is full yet wanes again. Sometimes he climbs the mountain grasping the nine-jointed staff; sometimes he stands by the water, lest he let it leak away.
The green mountains rise steeply, the white clouds are deep; atop the peak, the man from Silla [is] □□. □□.

Entrusting gold to another, the sun pierces through the Iron Kunlun; the jade hare illuminates the court as ancient trees divide the light. The straw dog barks at the stars as the constellations turn;
the clay ox bellows, heard by those with deaf ears. The sound of water and the song of forest birds harmonize together, until the great ocean is clear and transparent to its depths.
How dark it is! What need is there to wield the brush? I shall simply entrust this to you: wildflowers newly bloom from the spring of years past.
Ascending the mountain, its nine-tiered peaks tower loftily into the Great Void; though all things are manifold, there is but one true luminosity. Travelers must reach the solitary peak.
O Summit! Do not dwell in the middle or perceive inequality.
When the wind sings, the branches do not rustle; when the rain falls, it does not break clods of earth. Since the nature of sin is empty, you must diligently repent. Thus was Sumeru awakened.
It is the most supreme. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra form a pair. The clouds part to reveal the high peaks, where the ancient pines are green. Holding hands, I ask you: who would not understand?
Who would not understand? Not breaking the clod, not breaking the clod—*xi bázàisuì* (a hundredfold shattering)!

Seeing off Guest Attendant Ping, we shook hands and gazed at the heavens as he slept; how many mountain ranges lie within the forest clouds? When shall I lift a single strand of hair and stir the chill of the emerald pool?
— An admonition to my disciples.
How lamentable! A single speck of snow upon a red furnace. All things in this world are as insubstantial. Do not cherish the many trailing charms of lovely flowers;
they will surely not remain fresh before you for even a hundred days.

Seeing off the monk, the wind favors him; the iron sails are hoisted upon the sea vessel. The guest returns to Nanpu, where all worldly ties have ceased. The "Yajiao" youths sleep together in the mist-shrouded temple;
we walk side by side through the seclusion of the ancient ravine. Extending his arms, he tears open the canopy of the void; turning his body, he kicks the moon to pieces.
A bubble in the midst [of life]. Next year, the fragrant lichees will surely ripen in abundance. Do not remain in Wuzhou and climb the tower again.
Sing of yourself as white jade; do not compare it to common white stone. Use gold for what it is worth; do not trade it for yellow brass. If a man is truly a man...
Child, beauty and ugliness, high and low, all rest upon the eye. Let the peaks tilt and the myriad rivers surge; let there be long poles and hooks across the four seas.
Why do you smile alone when sleep comes? Brew tea with pine and bamboo and enjoy a single bowl.

Entrusting this to the virtue of the Sangha, its essence is spontaneously complete like the sands of the Ganges; yet for those lost in delusion, it requires five thousand leagues of treading through snow.
Although there are profound and wondrous aspects externally, when spring arrives, the grass grows green of itself.

Entrusting this to Elder Brother Zhao, we view the moon on the stream together; though the reflections differ, the fullness is one. The mountain passes of my old home are locked fast by layered clouds. The black hen crows with the moon as dawn breaks;
the straw dog barks at the cold of the Dipper. It is easy to cut straight through the fence, yet difficult for the lips to enter the mirror through winding paths.
One should raise this challenge: "Dragon Creek dewdrops fall beyond the tiered peaks; the round glow of the red sun is viewed from the north.
Snowflakes scatter like silver upon the peaks—the mechanism of Samantabhadra. Though the ancient path remains open, those who walk it are few. Do not speak of the black rooster adding a finger."
Commentary: The plum blossoms on the southern branch of the ridge have already bloomed first.
Without investigation, they spontaneously break through;
one need not use a hammer to shatter the vast sky. Why rely on further inserting a chisel at the gateway? Let others have their "superior existence"—Zhang Liang.
If you calculate, you will surely suffer loss upon returning without verification.
Daily activities scatter like shadows at midday; pluck the freshness from within the moon. Where hand and eye cannot reach, those who know the sound must step forward.
To Xu Longtu Ruzi:
From the beginning, your nature and mind have been wicked; were it not for Deshan, who would dare to strike you down?
A single phrase from Fachang no one knows—reaching out at random, he snaps a branch of coral. How truly marvelous! For fifty years, it has been sought but never found. [The Mirror of the Lips]
"Eh! Turning over, he kicks through the painted Mount Sumeru; dragging down space, he makes it a lid and a ground-covering.
A lion cub of equal caliber—if at some time he encounters the old man of Vaiśālī, a spike behind his head will pierce him, and his horns will clearly distinguish him as a true Maudgalyāyana."

Answer: Master Xu Longtu of Fanchang has a well-ordered old turtle-snout. Born thus, it comes and goes without front or back; it conceals its body while revealing its shadow as if it were not there at all.
To touch it is to have one’s very body pulverized. That donkey is even more extraordinary: its two ears hang down long, and its four legs...
He lands on the ground. He comes right like this, acting as if he were a snake breathing out its venom; the snake does not spare its own life.
As he approaches and lets out a sneeze, that old donkey is utterly witless.
Furthermore, he replied to Xu Longtu:
"The same wind blows over a thousand *li*; your Way is excellent. This is precisely 'casting one's body into the wild weeds.

Even if you were to manifest before the eyes of all people, I suspect you have still not seen the Old Huanglong. The sweatshirt next to the skin is new again and new; what of the hat from the Three Mountains?"
Once I was walking about with a waist-belt that had no buckles, its two ends hanging down; wearing bottomless hemp sandals that had never been worn through. Come, come!
I shall give you a gourd vine to plant upon a stone; next year you will harvest a great winter melon that neither swift axe nor sharp blade can cleave.
Hanshan claps his hands and laughs heartily, pointing out the Venerable Nanyue Huairang.
Entrusting this to Chan Master Nanshan of Huanglong:
The spring colors are lush and green as the orioles sing their songs; Peaches and plums, red and white, appear before many eyes. Who knows who will cherish Lingyun’s words?
Pointing toward the mountain, he comes down to pay his respects to me.

Seeing off a monk, the yellow chrysanthemums are fragrant while the green grasses wither. With a staff of rattan, he speaks of his southern return at the edge of the forest. One knows well that the old mountain peaks lack eternal stone;
alone, he closes his thatched gate facing the setting sun.
One day before the Master was about to pass away, he sent a verse to Xu Longtu, who was seventy-seven years old that year.
It read: "When setting out on a journey, one must choose an auspicious day. Last night I consulted Guige, and he reported that tomorrow morning would be the time."
The Master held the position for twenty-three years;
Xu Longtu composed this eulogy for his portrait:
"Who does not understand Chan? Yet he sought to be National Teacher. For twenty-three years, no one has dared to doubt him. The grass grows long and the snow melts away."
The spring is in full bloom. Entrust it to the ancient masters of all quarters.
The Elder of the Valleys and Mountains offers this verse:
"Every dharma has been fully traversed; it is like a reflection appearing in a mirror, or a gourd floating on water—press down and it turns immediately."
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yu of Fachang Chan Monastery (concluded).
I have observed those who realize the ground of the Dharma-nature, practice in accordance with that nature, and constantly take the Dharma as their delight.
Lao Fachang was such a man. Now I, Yuzhao, have carved his words for circulation and request a preface or colophon.
Thus, I have written this for him. By the Elder Lingyuan, Weiqing.
